{{Short description|Theorem in computational and discrete geometry}}
[[File:Zone theorem.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|The zone of a line (red) in an arrangement of lines, consisting of all faces that touch the given line]]
In [[geometry]], the '''zone theorem''' is a result that establishes the complexity of the zone of a line in an [[arrangement of lines]].

==Definition==

A ''line arrangement'', denoted as <math>A(L)</math>, is a subdivision of the plane, induced by a set of lines <math>L</math>, into cells (<math>2</math>-dimensional faces), edges (<math>1</math>-dimensional faces) and vertices (<math>0</math>-dimensional faces). Given a set of <math>n</math> lines <math>L</math>, the line arrangement <math>A(L)</math>, and a line <math>l</math> (not belonging to <math>L</math>), the ''zone'' of <math>l</math> is the set of faces intersected by <math>l</math>. The ''complexity'' of a zone is the total number of edges in its boundary, expressed as a function of <math>n</math>.
The zone theorem states that said complexity is [[Big O notation|<math>O(n)</math>]].

==History==

This result was published for the first time in 1985;<ref name="duality">{{harvtxt|Chazelle|Guibas|Lee|1985}}</ref> Chazelle et al. gave the [[Upper Bound|upper bound]] of <math>10n+2</math> for the complexity of the zone of a line in an arrangement. In 1991,<ref name = "horizon">{{harvtxt| Bern | Eppstein | Plassman | Yao|1991}}</ref> this bound was improved to <math>\lfloor9.5n\rfloor -1</math>, and it was also shown that this is the best possible upper bound up to a small additive factor. Then, in 2011,<ref>{{harvtxt| Pinchasi| 2011}}</ref> Rom Pinchasi  proved that the complexity of the zone of a line in an arrangement is at most <math>\lfloor9.5n\rfloor -3</math>, and this is a [[Upper and lower bounds|tight bound]].

Some paradigms used in the different proofs of the theorem are [[Mathematical induction|induction]],<ref name ="duality"/> [[plane sweep|sweep]] technique,<ref name = "horizon"/><ref>{{harvtxt| Edelsbrunner | O'Rourke | Seidel|1986}}</ref> [[Tree (graph theory)|tree]] construction,<ref>{{harvtxt| Edelsbrunner | Guibas| 1989}}</ref> and [[Davenport–Schinzel sequence|Davenport-Schinzel sequences]].<ref name="curves">{{harvtxt|Edelsbrunner|Guibas|Pach|Pollack|Seidel|Sharir|1992}}</ref><ref name="zone">{{harvtxt|Edelsbrunner|Seidel|Sharir|1991}}</ref>

==Generalizations==

Although the most popular version is for arrangements of lines in the plane, there exist some generalizations of the zone theorem. For instance, in dimension <math>d</math>, considering [[Arrangement of hyperplanes|arrangements of hyperplanes]], the complexity of the zone of a hyperplane <math>h</math> is the number of facets (<math>d-1</math> - dimensional faces) bounding the set of cells (<math>d</math>-dimensional faces) intersected by <math>h</math>. Analogously, the <math>d</math>-dimensional zone theorem states that the complexity of the zone of a hyperplane is <math>O(n^{d-1})</math>.<ref name="zone" />  There are considerably fewer proofs for the theorem for dimension <math>d\geq3</math>. For the <math>3</math>-dimensional case, there are proofs based on sweep techniques and for higher dimensions is used Euler's relation:<ref>{{harvtxt| Saxena| 2021}}</ref>
<math display="block">\sum_{i=0}^{d} (-1)^i F_i \geq 0. </math>

Another generalization is considering arrangements of [[pseudoline]]s (and [[pseudohyperplanes]] in dimension <math>d</math>) instead of lines (and hyperplanes). Some proofs for the theorem work well in this case since they do not use the straightness of the lines substantially through their arguments.<ref name="zone" />

==Motivation==

The primary motivation to study the zone complexity in arrangements arises from looking for efficient [[algorithm]]s to construct arrangements. A classical algorithm is the incremental construction, which can be roughly described as adding the lines one after the other and storing all faces generated by each in an appropriate [[data structure]] (the usual structure for arrangements is the [[Doubly connected edge list|doubly connected edge list (DCEL)]]). Here, the consequence of the zone theorem is that the entire construction of any arrangement of <math>n</math> lines can be done in time <math>O(n^2)</math>, since the insertion of each line takes time <math>O(n)</math>.
